items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: The last one that was here was my drummer, Fats Martin

ctx.x: No. The last one that was here was my drummer, Fats Martin, and he passed away, oh, about three or four years ago. Well, in fact, he took the remnants of my band and kept going when I gave up. And I stayed with him until he passed, and everybody knew him as a great drummer.
Is there anything else about the recording date, wherever those records made, for Vocalion? Here in town? Here in San Antonio.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-12-30
items.q: So I got Fats Martin which was a blessing in disguise. Because this guy turned out to be to me one of the greatest drummers that I'd ever heard.

ctx.x: Look, we never did call him Little Rock on the back. No, no. So I got Fats Martin which was a blessing in disguise. Because this guy turned out to be to me one of the greatest drummers that I'd ever heard. He had a bad tendency though to increase time sometimes. Well sometimes it was bad if we were playing a show similar to the one we played with in Detroit, Michigan. And he had this guy, Pete Peaches of Duke, had great, great dances out of the cotton club. But Pete had gone, Pete Nugent had gone and the singer.…
And of course that's, we just scratching the surface when we start talking about the foys of your band and everything. How many drummers have you known that didn't increase? How many of them?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: I consider Freddie one of the finest drummers that I've ever had the opportunity of working with. By the same token, I believe Fats was the greatest.

ctx.x: Yeah, but I've never heard Fats Martin in person. Do you think it's fair to Fats Martin or fair to the rest of the band? Is it true to the band's sound is what I'm getting at?
I think it is. Yeah. But however, it could be, it would make a lot better today.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1969-12-30
items.q: And Fats Martin picked up the remnants of my band and he just kept it at a level of five, six and seven pieces.

ctx.x: Yeah, you mentioned that that had to do with the breaking up of the band.

Well, that happened in the later, later years. I broke up that one time right after Al Travis said to give us that bad booking. And I came back to New Orleans. I thought I wanted to quit. So, I'm being before you, I thought that some Negro agent came here and could make a tremendous, a lot of money for his boy. And I tried to explain what type of deal this was, but he went ahead and he let me have $4,000. And this proved to be a bad booker. I had to get rid of him, so I wanted to still keep the band after going…
What about this Bernard Goldberg? Had you get in touch with him?
